summary: Slovenia is an EU and Schengen member: EU/EEA citizens enter freely with an ID card, around 60 visa-waiver nationalities — including the US, UK, Japan and most of the Americas — get 90 days in any 180 across the whole Schengen Area, and other travelers need a Schengen visa.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: Standard Schengen fee for adults; children aged 6–12 pay €45.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

fee.notes: Indicative fee for long-stay purposes (work, study, family) under Slovenian national rules. Confirm with the Slovenian embassy.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the previous 10 years. EU/EEA and Swiss citizens can enter with a passport or national ID card.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must show travel medical insurance with at least €30,000 of cover valid across the Schengen Area. Visa-waiver visitors are not checked, but cover is strongly recommended; EU citizens can use the EHIC.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

onwardTicket.text: Not routinely checked, but border officers may ask visa-waiver visitors about return plans, accommodation and means of support.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is systematically enforced; officers may ask non-EU visitors to show sufficient means for the stay — around €70 per day is commonly cited.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more must be declared when entering or leaving the EU. There are no controls at internal Schengen borders.

source.name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia — GOV.SI

notes: Standard EU allowances apply to alcohol and tobacco brought from outside the EU.

payments.text: Cards are accepted nearly everywhere, from Ljubljana cafés to Lake Bled boat rentals; a little cash is handy at farmers' markets, mountain huts and rural guesthouses.

safety.text: Slovenia is among the safest countries in Europe, with very low crime. The main risks are outdoors — fast-changing Alpine weather in the Julian Alps and busy summer roads to the coast.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Slovenia Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September is ideal for Lake Bled, Ljubljana and hiking in the Julian Alps; winter brings skiing at Kranjska Gora and quiet karst towns.

roadVignette.appliesTo: Vehicles up to 3.5 t. Toll class 2A covers most cars (up to 1.3 m high above the front axle); taller vans and campers pay class 2B, which is twice the price.

penalty.notes: Fine for using a motorway or expressway without a valid e-vignette.

roadVignette.text: Slovenian motorways and expressways run on an e-vignette linked to the number plate; vehicles without one may not enter a toll road. Two stretches sit outside it: the Karavanke tunnel to Austria, which costs €9 per crossing for a car at the Hrušica toll booth, and — since January 1, 2026 — the coastal H5 and H6 expressways, which no longer need a vignette at all.

source.name: DARS — E-vignette types, toll classes and prices

idp.text: Slovenia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties

driving.text: Slovenia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Slovenia yet.

tips.text: You need an e-vignette to drive on Slovenian motorways. Buy it online (evinjeta.dars.si) before crossing the border; camera enforcement issues heavy fines.
July and August crowds at Lake Bled and Vintgar Gorge are heavy — go early in the morning, or head to nearby Lake Bohinj for similar scenery with far fewer people.
Weather in the Julian Alps changes fast. Check forecasts, carry layers even in summer, and note that mountain rescue can be charged to uninsured hikers.
Visa-waiver nationals will need an ETIAS travel authorization once the EU system becomes mandatory. Check the official EU website for the current status before traveling.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Slovenia?
faq.answer: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 visa-waiver countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas — get 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area. Everyone else needs a Schengen visa from a Slovenian embassy or visa center.

faq.question: Is Slovenia in the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Yes, since 2007. There are no border checks when arriving from Italy, Austria, Hungary or Croatia (all Schengen members), and your 90/180-day visa-free allowance is shared across the whole area.

faq.question: Will I need ETIAS for Slovenia?
faq.answer: Once the EU's ETIAS system becomes mandatory, visa-waiver travelers will need the online authorization before their trip. It is expected to cost a small fee, be valid for three years, and cover the whole Schengen Area. Check the official EU site for the launch date.

faq.question: What currency does Slovenia use?
faq.answer: The euro, since 2007. Cards and contactless payments are accepted nearly everywhere.

faq.question: Can I day-trip from Slovenia to Croatia or Italy?
faq.answer: Yes, easily — both are Schengen members, so there are no border checks. Trieste, Zagreb and the Istrian coast are all within a couple of hours of Ljubljana. Remember that days anywhere in the Schengen Area count toward the same 90/180 allowance.
